statements.label: supported
statements.text: In the subgroup of patients who relapsed, ctDNA positivity was associated with shorter overall survival (hazard ratio 2.71).
statements.evidence: In patients who experienced recurrence, ctDNA positivity correlated with shorter OS (HR: 2.71, P < 0.0001).
statements.note: Among patients who experienced recurrence, ctDNA positivity correlated with shorter overall survival, with a hazard ratio of 2.71.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Spontaneous ctDNA clearance without clinical recurrence was more common in stage II colon cancer than in stage III disease.
statements.evidence: True spontaneous clearance rate with no clinical recurrence was 1.9% (2/105).
statements.note: The abstract gives only the overall spontaneous clearance rate (1.9%, 2 of 105) and does not break it down by stage.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Patients whose ctDNA clearance after adjuvant chemotherapy was sustained had 89.0% disease-free survival at 24 months, against 3.3% when clearance was only transient.
statements.evidence: Sustained ctDNA clearance in response to ACT was an indicator of favorable DFS and OS compared to transient clearance (24-month DFS: 89.0% versus 3.3%; 24-month OS: 100.0% versus 82.3%).
statements.note: The abstract reports 24-month disease-free survival of 89.0% with sustained ctDNA clearance on adjuvant chemotherapy versus 3.3% with transient clearance.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: During the MRD window, ctDNA positivity was tied to much worse disease-free survival (hazard ratio 11.99) and overall survival (hazard ratio 9.68).
statements.evidence: reinforces the prognostic value of ctDNA positivity during the MRD window with significantly inferior disease-free survival (DFS; hazard ratio (HR): 11.99, P < 0.0001) and overall survival (OS; HR: 9.68, P < 0.0001)
statements.note: In the updated analysis, ctDNA positivity in the MRD window carried hazard ratios of 11.99 for disease-free survival and 9.68 for overall survival.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Switching therapy for patients whose ctDNA stayed detectable after neoadjuvant chemotherapy improved their response and prognosis.
statements.evidence: On the basis of these findings, the I-SPY2 trial will prospectively test ctDNA for utility in redirecting therapy to improve response and prognosis.
statements.note: Redirecting therapy on the basis of ctDNA is only planned for future prospective testing; the abstract reports no results of doing so.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Triple-negative breast cancer patients had a higher ctDNA positivity rate than hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative patients before, during and after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
statements.evidence: ctDNA positivity rates before, during, and after NAC are higher in TNBC than in HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer patients.
statements.note: The abstract states that ctDNA positivity rates at all three time points around neoadjuvant chemotherapy were higher in TNBC than in HR-positive/HER2-negative disease.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Only in triple-negative breast cancer did clearing ctDNA by week 3 of treatment predict a favorable response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
statements.evidence: Early clearance of ctDNA 3 weeks after treatment initiation predicts a favorable response to NAC in TNBC only.
statements.note: The abstract restricts the predictive value of early (3-week) ctDNA clearance for neoadjuvant chemotherapy response to TNBC.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Being ctDNA-negative after neoadjuvant chemotherapy was linked to better outcomes, even for patients left with extensive residual cancer.
statements.evidence: Conversely, ctDNA negativity after NAC correlates with improved outcomes, even in patients with extensive residual cancer.
statements.note: The abstract reports that ctDNA negativity after neoadjuvant chemotherapy correlated with improved outcomes, including in patients with extensive residual cancer.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The ctDNA-based survival model picked out high-risk patients in an external validation cohort from the OAK trial, with an overall survival hazard ratio of 3.73.
statements.evidence: The model also identified high-risk patients in an external validation cohort from the randomized phase 3 OAK study of ICI versus chemo in NSCLC (OS HR = 3.73 (1.83-7.60), P = 0.00012).
statements.note: In the external OAK validation cohort, the model's high-risk group had an overall survival hazard ratio of 3.73.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Among patients with stable disease, those classed as high risk by ctDNA had shorter median overall survival than low-intermediate-risk patients, 7.1 versus 22.3 months.
statements.evidence: ctDNA assessments through cycle 3 day 1 of treatment enabled risk stratification of patients with stable disease (hazard ratio (HR) = 3.2 (2.0-5.3), P < 0.001; median 7.1 versus 22.3 months for high- versus low-intermediate risk)
statements.note: For patients with stable disease, ctDNA-based high-risk patients had a median overall survival of 7.1 months versus 22.3 months for low-intermediate-risk patients.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Switching high-risk patients identified by early ctDNA testing to a different therapy improved their overall survival.
statements.evidence: Overall, measuring ctDNA dynamics during treatment can improve patient risk stratification and may allow early differentiation between competing therapies during clinical trials.
statements.note: The abstract reports risk stratification and trial simulations, not the outcome of changing anyone's therapy on the basis of ctDNA.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Simulated clinical trials indicated that testing ctDNA early in treatment outperformed early radiographic imaging at predicting trial outcomes.
statements.evidence: Simulations of clinical trial scenarios employing our ctDNA model suggested that early ctDNA testing outperforms early radiographic imaging for predicting trial outcomes.
statements.note: The trial simulations suggested that early ctDNA testing predicts trial outcomes better than early radiographic imaging.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Routine dd-cfDNA monitoring reduced the number of kidney biopsies needed to diagnose allograft rejection.
statements.evidence: Our study provides insights on the potential value of assessing dd-cfDNA, in addition to standard of care monitoring, to improve the detection of allograft rejection.
statements.note: The abstract discusses better detection of rejection but reports nothing about how many biopsies were performed or avoided.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The association between dd-cfDNA and rejection was confirmed in external validation cohorts of 1,748 patients, including 439 African American patients.
statements.evidence: These results were confirmed in the external validation cohorts (n = 1,748) including a cohort of African American patients (n = 439).
statements.note: The abstract states the results were confirmed in external validation cohorts totalling 1,748 patients, among them a cohort of 439 African American patients.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Including dd-cfDNA in a standard-of-care prediction model increased the area under the curve from 0.777 to 0.821.
statements.evidence: The inclusion of dd-cfDNA to a standard of care prediction model showed improved discrimination (area under the curve 0.777 (95% CI 0.741-0.811) to 0.821 (95% CI 0.784-0.852); P = 0.0011) and calibration.
statements.note: Adding dd-cfDNA to the standard of care model raised the area under the curve from 0.777 to 0.821 (P = 0.0011).

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Antibody-mediated, T cell-mediated and mixed rejection were each strongly correlated with donor-derived cell-free DNA levels.
statements.evidence: Donor-derived cell-free DNA levels strongly correlated with allograft rejection, including antibody-mediated rejection (P < 0.0001), T cell-mediated rejection (P < 0.0001) and mixed rejection (P < 0.0001).
statements.note: The abstract reports strong correlations of dd-cfDNA levels with antibody-mediated, T cell-mediated and mixed rejection, each at P < 0.0001.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Using deep learning, MRD-EDGE SNV increased SNV signal-to-noise enrichment in WGS roughly 300-fold relative to previous WGS error suppression.
statements.evidence: MRD-EDGE SNV uses deep learning and a ctDNA-specific feature space to increase SNV signal-to-noise enrichment in WGS by ~300× compared to previous WGS error suppression.
statements.note: The abstract reports a ~300-fold rise in SNV signal-to-noise enrichment over previous WGS error suppression.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: With MRD-EDGE CNV, the aneuploidy required for ultrasensitive CNV detection through WGS dropped from 1 Gb to 200 Mb.
statements.evidence: MRD-EDGE CNV also reduces the degree of aneuploidy needed for ultrasensitive CNV detection through WGS from 1 Gb to 200 Mb
statements.note: The abstract states that MRD-EDGE CNV cuts the aneuploidy needed for ultrasensitive WGS-based CNV detection from 1 Gb to 200 Mb.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: MRD-EDGE SNV allowed disease monitoring from plasma alone, without tumor information, in advanced melanoma and lung cancer patients receiving immune-checkpoint inhibition.
statements.evidence: Finally, the radical signal-to-noise enrichment in MRD-EDGE SNV enables plasma-only (non-tumor-informed) disease monitoring in advanced melanoma and lung cancer, yielding clinically informative TF monitoring for patients on immune-checkpoint inhibition.
statements.note: The abstract reports plasma-only, non-tumor-informed monitoring in advanced melanoma and lung cancer, giving informative tumor fraction tracking during immune-checkpoint inhibition.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: After surgery, MRD-EDGE detected residual disease earlier than radiographic imaging did.
statements.evidence: We harness the improved performance to identify MRD following surgery in multiple cancer types, track changes in TF in response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in lung cancer and demonstrate ctDNA shedding in precancerous colorectal adenomas.
statements.note: The abstract says MRD was identified after surgery but makes no comparison with imaging and gives no lead time.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Treatment was changed for some patients in the study on the basis of their plasma epigenomic profiles.
statements.evidence: This proof-of-concept study in advanced cancers shows how plasma epigenomic profiling has the potential to unlock clinically actionable information that is currently accessible only via direct tissue sampling.
statements.note: The abstract speaks only of the potential to provide actionable information and reports no treatment decisions made from the profiles.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The researchers generated more than 1,200 plasma epigenomic profiles from 433 individuals with one of 15 cancer types.
statements.evidence: we measured 1,268 epigenomic profiles in plasma from 433 individuals with one of 15 cancers
statements.note: The abstract reports 1,268 plasma epigenomic profiles from 433 individuals with one of 15 cancers.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The assay served as a robust stand-in for transcriptional activity, letting the researchers infer expression levels of diagnostic markers and drug targets.
statements.evidence: Our assay provided a robust proxy for transcriptional activity, allowing us to infer the expression levels of diagnostic markers and drug targets
statements.note: The abstract states the assay was a robust proxy for transcriptional activity that allowed inference of diagnostic marker and drug target expression.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The researchers developed a method that comprehensively profiles the cancer epigenome using 1 ml of a patient's plasma.
statements.evidence: we developed a method for comprehensive epigenomic profiling of cancer from 1 ml of patient plasma
statements.note: The abstract describes a new method for comprehensive cancer epigenomic profiling from 1 ml of patient plasma.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The analysis drew on 738 plasma samples from 491 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, enrolled in two randomized phase II trials or a biobanking program.
statements.evidence: across 738 plasma samples from 491 male mCRPC patients from two randomized multicentre phase II trials and a prospective province-wide blood biobanking program
statements.note: The abstract states the analysis covered 738 plasma samples from 491 mCRPC patients drawn from two randomized phase II trials and a province-wide biobanking program.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Changing treatment on the basis of a high ctDNA fraction improved survival in men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.
statements.evidence: Our results affirm ctDNA% as an actionable tool for patient risk stratification and provide a practical framework for optimized biomarker testing.
statements.note: The abstract calls ctDNA% actionable for risk stratification but reports no outcome of changing treatment based on it.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: ctDNA fraction tracked serum and radiographic measures of disease burden and reached its highest values in patients with liver metastases.
statements.evidence: ctDNA% correlates with serum and radiographic metrics of disease burden and is highest in patients with liver metastases.
statements.note: The abstract reports that ctDNA% correlates with serum and radiographic disease-burden metrics and is highest in patients with liver metastases.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Regardless of treatment context, ctDNA fraction predicted overall survival, progression-free survival and treatment response better than established clinical prognostic factors.
statements.evidence: ctDNA% strongly predicts overall survival, progression-free survival, and treatment response independent of therapeutic context and outperformed established prognostic clinical factors.
statements.note: The abstract states ctDNA% predicted survival and response independent of therapeutic context and outperformed established prognostic clinical factors.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In the independent validation set, MCDBT-1 reached 69.1% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity, and identified tissue of origin with 83.2% accuracy.
statements.evidence: MCDBT-1 yielded a sensitivity of 69.1% (64.8%-73.3%), a specificity of 98.9% (97.6%-99.7%), and tissue origin accuracy of 83.2% (78.7%-87.1%) in the independent validation set.
statements.note: The abstract reports 69.1% sensitivity, 98.9% specificity and 83.2% tissue-of-origin accuracy for MCDBT-1 in the independent validation set.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: For patients with stage I-III cancer, MCDBT-1 detected cancer with a sensitivity of 59.8%.
statements.evidence: For early-stage (I-III) patients, the sensitivity of MCDBT-1 was 59.8% (54.4%-65.0%).
statements.note: The abstract gives a sensitivity of 59.8% for MCDBT-1 in early-stage (I-III) patients.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: MCDBT-1 detected pancreatic cancer with greater sensitivity than lung cancer.
statements.evidence: In the real-world simulation, MCDBT-1 achieved a sensitivity of 70.6% in detecting the six cancers
statements.note: The abstract gives only sensitivities pooled across the six cancers and no figures for individual cancer types.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: For populations at relatively high cancer risk, MCDBT-2 offered a higher sensitivity than MCDBT-1, 75.1%, with a specificity of 95.1%.
statements.evidence: MCDBT-2 was generated at a slightly low specificity of 95.1% (92.8%-96.9%) but a higher sensitivity of 75.1% (71.9%-79.8%) than MCDBT-1 for populations at relatively high risk of cancers
statements.note: The abstract reports that MCDBT-2, aimed at higher-risk populations, had 75.1% sensitivity, above that of MCDBT-1, at a specificity of 95.1%.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Non-canonical personalized variants made up 98.2% of the variants and showed prognostic effects comparable to those of canonical variants.
statements.evidence: Personalized non-canonical variants account for 98.2% with prognostic effects similar to canonical variants.
statements.note: The abstract states that personalized non-canonical variants account for 98.2% and have prognostic effects similar to canonical variants.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: PROPHET detected molecular residual disease a median of 299 days ahead of radiologically confirmed recurrence.
statements.evidence: It outperforms fixed-panel assays in prognostic analysis and demonstrates a median lead-time of 299 days to radiologically confirmed recurrence.
statements.note: The abstract reports a median lead time of 299 days between PROPHET detection and radiologically confirmed recurrence.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: At baseline, PROPHET reached a ctDNA detection sensitivity of 45%, higher than that of the state-of-the-art fixed-panel assays.
statements.evidence: PROPHET and state-of-the-art fixed-panel assays were applied to 760 plasma samples from 181 prospectively enrolled early stage non-small cell lung cancer patients. PROPHET shows higher sensitivity of 45% at baseline with circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).
statements.note: PROPHET was run alongside fixed-panel assays, and the abstract reports its higher baseline ctDNA sensitivity of 45%.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Among patients PROPHET classified as MRD-positive, adjuvant therapy lengthened recurrence-free survival.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Clonal hematopoiesis variants produced false-positive MRD calls in some patients during chemoradiotherapy.
statements.evidence: Further analysis revealed that pretreatment ctDNA variants serve as an essential MRD informed source.
statements.note: The abstract says pretreatment ctDNA variants are an essential source for MRD calling but mentions nothing about clonal hematopoiesis or false positives.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The 38 patients (27.3%) with undetectable ctDNA both on-RT and after RT had better survival, whether or not they received consolidation immune checkpoint inhibitors.
statements.evidence: Thirty-eight (27.3%) patients with early undetectable ctDNA at both on-RT (RT reached 40 Gy) and after-RT time points, indicating early response to CRT, had better survival outcomes for both with or without consolidation immune checkpoint inhibitors.
statements.note: The abstract reports better survival for the 38 (27.3%) early ctDNA-undetectable patients both with and without consolidation immune checkpoint inhibitors.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Patients whose MRD stayed undetectable over time, 20.1% of the cohort, reached a 2-year cancer-specific progression-free survival of 88.4%.
statements.evidence: Longitudinal undetectable MRD was found in 20.1% patients. The 2-year cancer-specific progression-free survival of these patients was 88.4%
statements.note: The abstract reports longitudinally undetectable MRD in 20.1% of patients and a 2-year cancer-specific progression-free survival of 88.4% in this group.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: As chemoradiotherapy proceeded, ctDNA concentrations decreased significantly at the on-RT and after-RT time points relative to baseline.
statements.evidence: ctDNA concentrations showed a significantly declining trend as CRT progressed at on-RT and after-RT time points versus baseline.
statements.note: The abstract reports a significant decline in ctDNA concentrations at on-RT and after-RT time points compared with baseline.
